vignette:
Malee Siriwan is a seventy-six-year-old Vietnamese-Thai American woman who has worked as a mechanic for most of her adult life, a trade she learned from her father and carried with her through decades of immigration, marriage, and reinvention. She and her husband live in a modest home on the outskirts of a mid-sized Southern city, and until roughly eighteen months ago, she described her life as quietly satisfying - her days spent under cars, her evenings in the garden she kept along the back fence. That garden, and what happened in it, is where her current suffering begins.

The stalking began gradually, as it often does. A man she had known peripherally through a neighborhood association began appearing with increasing frequency near her property - at the edge of the lot when she worked in the yard, idling in a vehicle outside her shop, eventually leaving objects at her fence line. For several months Malee minimized what she was experiencing, attributing his presence to coincidence. The turning point came on an afternoon when she was kneeling in the soil behind her house, her hands in the earth and the smell of turned garden soil thick in the air, when she looked up and found him standing at the gate watching her. He said nothing. He did not need to. She understood in that moment, with a clarity she has never been able to fully articulate, that she was not safe. She called out; he walked away slowly, without urgency, as though he wanted her to understand that leaving was his choice. The incident was reported to police and eventually resolved legally, but Malee has not recovered.

What troubles her most now is the way memory operates - or fails to. When she attempts to recount what happened, particularly that afternoon in the garden, she loses the thread mid-sentence, trails off, and cannot finish. She has described this to her husband as feeling like the story dissolves before she reaches the end of it. At other times, she finds herself pushing the memory away before it can fully form, a reflex she does not entirely control. Yet when the memory does arrive, it arrives with terrible vividness - not as a narrative but as a series of frozen images, photographic and exact: his face at the gate, his hands at his sides, the particular angle of the afternoon light. These fragments surface without warning, and when they do, they pull her immediately back into a state of acute threat. The sense that danger is present and immediate floods her body before any conscious reasoning can intervene, and she finds herself scanning the room, checking behind her, listening for sounds she cannot name.

The triggers that activate this cycle are specific and, to Malee, bewildering in their reach. The smell of soil - encountered every time she passes the raised beds she no longer tends, or when a customer's vehicle carries mud from a rural job - returns her instantly to that afternoon. She cannot smell the earth without the photographs appearing in her mind, and once they appear, her body responds as though the threat is current. More distressing still is what happens when she is under stress at the shop, or in the rare moments when she allows herself to feel relaxed or even happy. Those states, which should be neutral or welcome, have become destabilizing - as though her nervous system has learned to treat any emotional arousal as a signal that something is about to go wrong. Feeling happy, she has come to believe, is a warning.

The threat monitoring has become constant. At work, she checks behind her when she hears footsteps on the shop floor. She has told her husband she feels on guard even inside their home, particularly near the windows that face the back yard. This vigilance, exhausting as it is, feeds back into the memory: the act of scanning and checking keeps her attention fixed on danger, and the images return more readily, which in turn makes the triggers more sensitive and the monitoring more urgent. The loop has been tightening for months.

What finally brought her to seek help was a morning when a customer brought in a truck caked in field mud, and she froze completely at the lift - unable to work, unable to explain why. She is hoping, she says carefully, to be able to go back into her garden. What she is most afraid of is that she no longer can.
